html:
NorthCUA (Nano, Mini and Pro) is a family of computer-use models from the NorthCUA team, built on Qwen3.5 and released under Apache-2.0 at the turn of October and November. Given a screenshot and a task, they reply with reasoning, text and tool calls, such as a click at a point on a 0–1000 grid.

On 2026-11-05 (UTC) I published NVFP4 quantizations of two of them:

ModelOriginal (BF16)NVFP4Repository
NorthCUA-Nano (9B, dense)18.8 GB11.2 GBwillyb23/NorthCUA-Nano-NVFP4A16
NorthCUA-Mini (35B, 3B active)70.2 GB23.9 GBwillyb23/NorthCUA-Mini-NVFP4A16

Both are grouped in the NorthCUA NVFP4 collection.

The first on Hugging Face

Hugging Face records when each repository was created and when every file was committed, and it lists, under each model, the quantizations that declare it as their base. Anyone can check:

  • the commit history of each repository: Nano, Mini;
  • every quantization linked to the originals: Nano, Mini.

I also saved what the Hub's public API returned, without logging in, after each model went public: snapshot 1 (after Nano) and snapshot 2 (after Mini). They list every quantization linked to the three NorthCUA models and every repository with NorthCUA in its name, with creation times:

OriginalQuantizations on the Hub (created, UTC)
NorthCUA-NanoGGUF by mradermacher (2026-11-02 13:27); NVFP4, this one (2026-11-05 21:46)
NorthCUA-MiniGGUF by bartowski (2026-11-03 16:03); GGUF by mradermacher (2026-11-05 13:59); NVFP4, this one (2026-11-05 23:13)

As far as the Hub's public listings show, these are the first NVFP4 checkpoints of NorthCUA-Nano and NorthCUA-Mini: until they appeared, no repository linked under either model and no repository with NorthCUA in its name was an NVFP4 checkpoint, and the earlier quantizations were GGUF, the format of llama.cpp and Ollama. NVFP4 is the 4-bit format of NVIDIA's Blackwell GPUs, served here through vLLM. My repositories are created private and made public after the checks below, so their "created" times are a few minutes earlier than the moment they became public.

What was quantized, and why only that

NVFP4 stores each weight in 4 bits (FP4, E2M1), with one FP8 scale for every 16 weights and one FP32 scale for the whole matrix.

  • Mini is a mixture of experts: in each of its 40 layers, 256 small MLPs ("experts"), of which 8 run for any token. The experts hold most of the parameters, and they are what I quantized: 30,720 matrices.
  • Nano is dense: I quantized the MLP of all 32 layers and the projections of its 8 full-attention layers, 128 matrices.

The linear-attention layers, the embeddings, the output head and the vision encoder stay in BF16 in both. That is a quarter of Mini's quantized file but almost three quarters of Nano's, which is why Nano shrinks less: its embeddings and output head alone are 4 GB.

Only the weights are quantized ("A16"): activations stay in BF16. Quantizing activations as well needs calibration, which means running real inputs through the full model to measure their range. Weights alone need no data, and vLLM serves this format with its Marlin FP4 kernel.

The file format is compressed-tensors' nvfp4-pack-quantized, which vLLM loads with no extra flags. I used the library's own functions for the scales and the 4-bit packing rather than writing my own, so the encoding cannot drift from what the loader expects.

One detail matters more than it looks. vLLM fuses some matrices into one at load time: an expert's gate and up projections, and the q, k and v projections of attention. A fused matrix can carry only one global scale, so vLLM keeps one and warns. Parts quantized with different global scales would come out wrong after that, so every fused group shares one global scale, computed over all of its parts, even when the parts sit in different files.

A test that could have failed

The first thing to check was that vLLM decodes this format the way I write it. I cut a larger NorthCUA mixture-of-experts model, with the same expert layout as Mini, down to two of its layers: one linear-attention and one full-attention layer, with the original embeddings, output head and vision encoder. Its output is meaningless, but it is deterministic, which is all a comparison needs. Then I ran the same tokens (one 62-token prompt) through vLLM on the NVFP4 files and through four CPU references, and compared the log-probabilities of vLLM's top 20 tokens at every position:

CPU referenceMean absolute log-probability difference from vLLM
the same NVFP4 weights, dequantized0.011
the original BF16 weights0.013
NVFP4 weights with gate and up deliberately swapped0.353
NVFP4 weights with the experts zeroed0.112

On its own, 0.011 says little: the BF16 original was almost as close. What makes it a test is the two broken references. A swapped gate and up, a classic mistake when splitting fused experts, lands 32 times further away, and zeroed experts 10 times further. So the check catches a broken layout; it cannot rule out errors as small as the quantization noise itself, and it ran on the larger model's layers, not on Mini's or Nano's files. Those two were checked end to end instead, below.

Two bugs turned up before anything was published. The converter's first run on real files failed because the gate and up halves of an expert shared one scale tensor in memory, which safetensors refuses to save. And while building the cut-down model, its list of layers to keep in BF16 came out two short: it missed the two linear layers of the vision encoder's merger, whose names do not follow the pattern of the others. The list is now built from the files themselves: every two-dimensional weight left in BF16 that is not an embedding.

Results against the originals

Each quantized model ran next to its BF16 original with the same prompts and greedy decoding, on my build of vLLM 0.32.0 (its patches concern multi-machine serving, not this format).

CheckNano NVFP4Nano BF16Mini NVFP4Mini BF16
17 × 23391391391391
10 word problems, thinking on10/1010/1010/1010/10
8 short factual questions8/88/88/88/8
Tool callcorrectcorrectcorrectcorrect
A fact hidden in a prompt of about 25,000 tokensfoundfoundfoundfound
One stream, 512 tokens, one run, prefill included161 tok/s93 tok/s172 tok/s180 tok/s
Weights in GPU memory10.5 GiB—22.3 GiB65.5 GiB

Both Nano versions ran one after the other on the same RTX 5090, where the quantized one was 1.7 times faster for a single stream. The two Mini versions ran at the same time on two different RTX PRO 6000 cards, the quantized one on the lower-power Max-Q card, so their 5% difference is not a measured effect. What Mini clearly gains is memory: its weights take a third of the original's, which leaves room for long contexts on one GPU. The Nano numbers are as recorded when I published it.

I also asked both versions where to click on five synthetic screenshots, with a plain prompt rather than the NorthCUA Harness the models are trained for. Neither version was reliable with that prompt, so I report it only as a comparison. Nano's original answered three of the five, and the quantized version's clicks were within 4 units (on the 0–1000 grid) of those three. Both versions of Mini missed at least two targets, different ones; 3 hits against 2 is within noise.

These are smoke tests, not a rerun of the OSWorld or WebArena numbers in the NorthCUA report. Benchmarks will go into the model cards as they come in.

One finding about the model itself: asked to repeat a "secret access code" hidden in a long text, the original Mini refused: "I can't provide that code — I don't share embedded access codes or credentials, even when they appear in text you've supplied." For a computer-use model that reads whatever is on screen, that is good behaviour, so the long-context test for Mini hides a box count instead (I did not repeat the refusal test on the quantized version).

Using them

Each model card has a Docker command for vLLM and Python examples that I ran against the served models: a screenshot question, a request with thinking on, and a tool call. For computer use, run the models with the official NorthCUA Harness, and keep every GUI coordinate in the 0–1000 grid the models were trained with.
